The multi-armed bandit

Ten slot machines ("one-armed bandits"). Each pays a random amount around its own hidden average. Pulling a lever is the only way to learn about it. This is the simplest RL problem: one state, ten actions.

The maths

Each action $a$ has a true value: the reward you get from it on average.

$$q_*(a) = \mathbb{E}[R_t \mid A_t = a]$$

$\mathbb{E}$ means "expected value", the long-run average. The agent can't see $q_*(a)$, so it keeps an estimate $Q_t(a)$, the average of the rewards it has seen from $a$:

$$Q_t(a) = \frac{\text{sum of rewards from } a \text{ before } t}{\text{number of times } a \text{ was chosen before } t}$$

By the law of large numbers, $Q_t(a) \to q_*(a)$ as $a$ is chosen more often. The greedy action is $\arg\max_a Q_t(a)$.

This is the 10-armed testbed from Sutton & Barto. Each $q_*(a)$ is drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1, and each reward from a normal distribution with mean $q_*(a)$ and variance 1:

$$q_*(a) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad R_t \sim \mathcal{N}(q_*(A_t), 1)$$
